text:
A FICO score is a number from 300 to 850. Most U.S. mortgage and card lenders use it. It sums up your credit file using five factors, each with a different weight.

1. **Payment history (35%).** This is the biggest factor. One payment that is 30 days late stays on your record for seven years. It can cut dozens of points from an otherwise clean profile.

2. **Amounts owed (30%).** The key measure here is your credit utilization ratio, which compares your balances to your credit limits. Balances above 30% of your limits suggest financial strain. Balances in the single digits suggest you have room to spare.

3. **Length of credit history (15%).** Older accounts that you keep open earn you credit over time.

4. **New credit and credit mix (20% combined).** Applying for many new accounts in a short time creates a burst of hard inquiries. Lenders may read that as a sign of desperation.

Many applicants think their salary matters. It doesn't. The model never sees your income, only your behavior.

If you put your statements on autopay and rarely apply for new credit, your score will climb steadily. Over time, the algorithm also forgives older blemishes.
